title: Chapter 12 Drill: Evidence, Outcomes, Ethics, and Radiology

items.stem: A surgical resident sustains a needlestick injury from a patient known to have chronic hepatitis B infection. The resident was vaccinated and has a documented protective antibody titer. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Wash the site and report it; no treatment because immunity is documented
Give hepatitis B immune globulin and start a full new vaccine series today
Begin antiviral therapy for six months
Isolate the resident from all clinical duties
items.explanation: A vaccinated person with a documented protective antibody response needs no prophylaxis after exposure to hepatitis B. The resident should still wash the site, report promptly, and have baseline testing and follow-up for other bloodborne pathogens as indicated. Immune globulin and boosters are for nonimmune individuals. Treatment is not indicated, and isolation has no justification.

items.stem: After a laparotomy, a sponge count is reported correct, yet an abdominal film taken for pain two days later shows a radiopaque marker in the pelvis. Which classification applies to this event?
options: An accepted complication of the operation, reported only if the patient asks
A planned second-look finding
An expected foreign body reaction
A never event, requiring disclosure and root cause analysis
items.explanation: A retained surgical item is a never event: a serious, largely preventable error that should not occur and triggers disclosure to the patient, reporting, removal, and a root cause analysis of counting and checking processes. Calling it a routine complication hides a system failure. It was not a planned second look. Foreign body reaction describes the tissue response, not the nature of the error.

items.stem: In a trial of a new surgical mesh, the hernia recurrence rate is 10 percent with standard repair and 6 percent with the new mesh. How many patients must receive the new mesh to prevent one recurrence?
options: Four
Twenty-five
Ten
Forty
items.explanation: The absolute risk reduction is 10 percent minus 6 percent, or 4 percent, and the number needed to treat is its reciprocal: one divided by 0.04, which equals 25. Four is the percentage difference itself, not its reciprocal. Ten and forty are not derived from these figures. A small absolute risk reduction produces a large number needed to treat even when the relative reduction looks impressive.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man is scheduled for a left inguinal hernia repair. In the holding area, the consent form and the site mark indicate the right side. What should happen next?
options: Proceed on the side that the surgeon personally prefers to operate on
Proceed and correct the form afterward
Stop and resolve the discrepancy before proceeding
Ask the anesthetist to decide the side
items.explanation: The universal protocol requires preprocedure verification, site marking, and a time-out in which every team member confirms patient, procedure, and side. Any discrepancy among the consent, mark, and schedule stops the process until it is resolved with the patient and records. Proceeding on preference or paperwork repair afterward risks wrong-site surgery. The anesthetist does not decide the operative side.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 28 needs contrast-enhanced computed tomography for suspected abdominal abscess. Which measure best reduces the risk of contrast-associated kidney injury?
options: Isotonic fluid, minimal contrast volume, and holding nephrotoxins
Oral diuretics given before the scan to flush the contrast out quickly
Prophylactic oral steroids on the day of the scan
Avoiding all imaging and relying on examination
items.explanation: Risk is lowered by volume expansion with isotonic crystalloid, the smallest effective dose of low-osmolar contrast, and temporary withdrawal of nephrotoxins such as anti-inflammatory drugs. Diuretics worsen volume depletion. Steroids are used to prevent allergic-type reactions, not kidney injury. When the study is clinically needed, denying it risks missing a drainable abscess, so the benefit is weighed against a modest and reducible renal risk.

items.stem: A resident realizes that a medication dose given to a patient the previous day was ten times too high, causing mild sedation without lasting harm. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Say nothing to anyone, since there was no lasting harm to the patient at all
Disclose honestly to the patient, report the event, and join the review
Alter the chart so the dose appears correct
Blame the pharmacy in the note
items.explanation: Ethical practice requires prompt, honest disclosure of an error to the patient or surrogate, an apology, and a report to the institution so system causes can be analyzed, even when harm is minor. Concealment erodes trust and prevents learning. Altering the record is falsification and a serious offense. Blaming another department in the record is inaccurate and unprofessional.

items.stem: Investigators want to determine whether a rare complication is linked to a prior exposure. They identify patients who developed the complication and a matched group who did not, then review past records for the exposure. Which design is this?
options: Prospective cohort study following patients forward
Randomized controlled trial assigning the exposure
Case-control study, looking back at exposure
Cross-sectional survey at a single time point
items.explanation: A case-control study begins with outcome status, selects cases and controls, and looks backward for exposure, which makes it efficient for rare outcomes and yields odds ratios. A prospective cohort follows exposed and unexposed groups forward. A randomized trial assigns the intervention. A cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at one moment. Case-control designs are prone to recall and selection bias.

items.stem: A surgical department reviews its operations and finds that patients with greater comorbidity have more complications. Leaders want to compare their performance fairly with other hospitals. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Risk-adjust outcomes, then compare observed with expected rates
Compare unadjusted raw complication rates across all of the hospitals
Exclude all high-risk patients from reporting
Report only the best surgeon's results
items.explanation: Risk adjustment, as used by quality programs like the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program, models expected outcomes from patient characteristics and compares them with observed results, giving an observed-to-expected ratio. Raw rates penalize centers that treat sicker patients. Excluding high-risk patients distorts the data and encourages avoidance of needed care. Selective reporting is misleading and unethical.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain and fever. Which imaging study is the best first test for suspected acute cholecystitis?
options: Noncontrast magnetic resonance imaging of the head
Plain radiograph of the abdomen
Positron emission tomography of the whole body
Right upper quadrant ultrasound
items.explanation: Ultrasound is the first-line study for biliary disease because it detects gallstones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and a sonographic Murphy sign without radiation. Plain films miss most gallstones. Head imaging is unrelated. Positron emission tomography is not used for acute biliary inflammation. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy is a second-line test when ultrasound is equivocal, and computed tomography is reserved for complications or alternative diagnoses.

items.stem: A surgical resident has worked beyond duty-hour limits for several days and admits to nodding off during a long case. What does the principle of fatigue management require?
options: Working through fatigue to prove commitment to the team and program
Using stimulants and caffeine to stay awake during long operations
Follow duty-hour limits, rest, and handoffs, in a culture allowing stepping away
Ignoring the limits during elective cases
items.explanation: Fatigue degrades judgment, vigilance, and technical performance, so programs enforce duty-hour limits, protected rest, structured handoffs, and a safety culture in which trainees can report impairment without penalty. Working through exhaustion raises error risk. Stimulants are not a substitute for rest. Duty-hour rules apply to elective and emergency work alike, and supervisors share responsibility for enforcing them and for covering the schedule.

items.stem: A hospital finds that 30-day readmission after colectomy is higher than that of peers. Which action is most likely to reduce preventable readmissions?
options: Structured discharge planning with early follow-up and clear instructions
Shortening hospital stays for all patients
Discouraging patients from calling after discharge
Limiting follow-up to a single clinic visit about six months after discharge
items.explanation: Readmission reduction depends on better transitions of care: medication reconciliation, teach-back education, early postoperative contact, and clear return precautions, with attention to ileus, dehydration, and wound problems. Shortening stays without support can raise readmissions. Discouraging calls delays recognition of complications. A single visit at six months misses the early window when most problems arise, and clear written instructions reduce avoidable calls and emergency visits.

items.stem: A surgeon wants to use a procedure code that pays more than the operation actually performed, since the extra time was devoted to the case. What is the correct approach?
options: Bill the higher code because the case ran long and took extra effort
Code only the documented, performed service; misrepresenting it is fraud
Split the service into several separate claims to raise the total payment received
Leave documentation vague so any code can apply
items.explanation: Billing must reflect the service actually performed and documented, and choosing a higher-paying code or unbundling to raise payment is a form of false claims fraud with legal and professional consequences. Case length alone does not justify a different code. Separating bundled components inflates payment. Vague documentation undermines valid coding and invites penalties on review, whereas accurate notes protect both the surgeon and the patient record.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man needs an elective hernia repair. The surgeon explains the procedure but does not discuss mesh complications or alternatives, and the patient signs the form without questions. Which element of informed consent is missing?
options: Verification of the patient's insurance coverage
Permission to photograph the operation
Confirmation of the surgeon's board certification and hospital privileges
Disclosure of material risks, benefits, and reasonable alternatives
items.explanation: Valid consent requires capacity, voluntariness, and adequate disclosure of the nature of the procedure, material risks, expected benefits, and reasonable alternatives including no treatment, with an opportunity for questions. A signature alone is not consent. Insurance verification, photography permission, and credentials are separate matters that do not make up the legal elements of the process.

items.stem: During a laparoscopic operation, the surgeon activates an electrosurgical instrument and flames appear near the drape at the patient's face while supplemental oxygen is flowing. What is the correct first response?
options: Continue operating and call for help afterward
Stop the oxygen, remove burning material, and extinguish the fire
Pour saline on the patient's face before doing anything else first
Increase the oxygen to flush the airway
items.explanation: An airway fire requires immediate cessation of the gases that feed the fire, removal of the endotracheal tube or burning drapes, and extinguishing with saline or a hand extinguisher, followed by reestablishing the airway and assessing injury. The three elements of the fire triangle are an oxidizer, fuel, and an ignition source. Increasing oxygen feeds the fire. Continuing to operate harms the patient.

items.stem: Researchers compare survival after two cancer operations in which some patients are lost to follow-up before the study ends. Which method best estimates survival while accounting for these patients?
options: Paired t test comparing mean survival times between groups
Chi-square test comparing crude death counts only
Linear regression of patient age on survival time
Kaplan-Meier estimation with log-rank comparison
items.explanation: Kaplan-Meier analysis handles censored data by using each patient's follow-up time up to the point of loss, and the log-rank test compares curves between groups. A t test assumes complete continuous data. Chi-square comparison of crude deaths ignores time and censoring. Linear regression of age is not a survival method. Cox proportional hazards models adjust for covariates.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man dies after an elective colectomy complicated by anastomotic leak. The surgical department convenes a monthly conference to review the case, examine contributing factors, and identify system improvements. Which principle should guide this morbidity and mortality review?
options: Assign individual blame to the operating surgeon alone, to deter errors
Avoid documenting contributing factors
Focus on systems and learning in a protected, nonpunitive setting
Share patient names with the media
items.explanation: Effective morbidity and mortality conferences identify errors and system contributors in a confidential peer review setting that protects candor, then translate findings into changes in process. Assigning blame discourages reporting. Failing to document contributing factors wastes the lesson. Disclosing patient identities violates privacy law. A just culture balances accountability with learning, and the lessons are shared across the department and hospital.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman with moderate dementia is admitted with a bowel obstruction needing surgery. She cannot describe her condition or weigh options, and has no advance directive. Her adult son and daughter disagree about surgery. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Identify the legal surrogate and use substituted judgment, with ethics help if conflict persists
Operate based on the surgeon's preference alone
Follow whichever relative speaks first
Delay care until the family agrees, regardless of risk
items.explanation: When a patient lacks capacity, the surrogate designated by law or by the usual hierarchy decides using substituted judgment, which is what the patient would have chosen, and then best interest if wishes are unknown. Family conflict warrants ethics support and communication. Surgeon preference alone ignores the patient's values. Following the first speaker has no standing. Indefinite delay risks harm in an emergency.

items.stem: A surgeon notices that a senior colleague has slurred speech, unsteady gait, and repeated near misses in the operating room. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Ignore it to avoid damaging the friendship
Confront the colleague loudly in front of patients and operating room staff
Wait until a patient is harmed before acting
Report through the proper channel to protect patients and help the peer
items.explanation: Physicians have an ethical duty to protect patients from an impaired colleague, so concerns are reported to the chief, impaired physician program, or medical staff leadership, which also directs the colleague toward evaluation and help. Ignoring the behavior risks patient safety. Public confrontation is unprofessional. Waiting for harm violates the duty to act on reasonable concern.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with abdominal pain is found to have an ovarian mass on ultrasound. She is 10 weeks pregnant and needs further imaging. Which modality is preferred for further cross-sectional evaluation without ionizing radiation?
options: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
Positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography
Magnetic resonance imaging without gadolinium contrast
Fluoroscopic contrast study of the bowel
items.explanation: In pregnancy, ultrasound is first and magnetic resonance imaging is preferred for additional cross-sectional detail because it uses no ionizing radiation, and gadolinium is avoided because it crosses the placenta. Computed tomography, PET with computed tomography, and fluoroscopy expose the fetus to ionizing radiation, though a necessary study should not be withheld when the benefit to the mother is clear.

items.stem: A new blood test for pancreatic cancer is evaluated in 200 patients. Of 50 with cancer, 45 test positive. Of 150 without cancer, 30 test positive. What is the sensitivity of the test?
options: Ninety percent
Eighty percent
Seventy-five percent
Sixty percent
items.explanation: Sensitivity is the proportion of diseased patients who test positive: 45 of 50, or 90 percent. Specificity is 120 of 150, or 80 percent, because 30 healthy patients tested positive. The positive predictive value is 45 of 75, or 60 percent. Seventy-five percent is not any of the computed values. Sensitivity helps rule out disease when high, whereas specificity helps rule in disease when high.

items.stem: A small randomized trial finds no significant difference in infection rates between two skin closure techniques, yet the true difference is later shown to be clinically important. Which error occurred, and what most likely caused it?
options: Type I error, most likely from testing multiple outcomes in one trial
Type II error, from inadequate sample size and low power
Selection bias, most likely from lack of randomization in assignment
Type I error, most likely from a very small p value
items.explanation: Failing to detect a real difference is a type II error, whose probability is beta, and power equals one minus beta. It most often results from too few participants. A type I error means declaring a difference that does not exist, which can come from multiple comparisons or chance. Randomization addresses selection bias. A negative trial should report power and confidence intervals so readers can judge it.
